passage:
Monday: Keerthana waited all evening for Ganga to return the statistics notes she had borrowed. They never came. Keerthana stewed, typing and deleting an angry message.
Wednesday: Before she could send it, Ganga knocked on her hostel door holding the notes and a packet of murukku. "I messed up, and you lost a day of revision. I'm sorry. Tell me if it hurt." Keerthana admitted it had. Ganga didn't argue or make it about herself; she listened and nodded.
The next Monday: Ganga turned up at eight sharp to study, as promised. When they disagreed about splitting the project, Ganga said, "Let's both write a plan and pick the better bits." No slammed books, no cold shoulder. Keerthana caught herself thinking, I want to disagree like that.

qa.q: What did Ganga bring when she came to Keerthana's door?
qa.a: She brought the notes and a packet of murukku.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling on Monday evening, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She was hurt and annoyed; she stewed all evening, typing and deleting an angry message.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the week, and why did it matter?
qa.a: Ganga came on her own to admit the mistake and asked how much it hurt, which repaired trust before it became a bigger fight.

qa.q: How might Ganga feel about the way she handled her mistake?
qa.a: She probably found it uncomfortable to admit, but she stayed calm enough to listen without arguing, as if she trusts a mistake can be mended.

grounding: Over a week, a student notices how a friend admits a mistake, keeps her promise and settles a disagreement calmly, and wants to learn from it.

passage: Sit, beta. Your Bhavna aunty will tell you about Deepak, my friend from engineering college in Nagpur, back when we were twenty. Deepak was not the cleverest in our group, but if he said he'd come at six to help with a drawing sheet, he came at six. Once, in third year, I shouted at him because he had told our friends about my failed exam. He went pale. Next day he found me in the canteen and said, "I broke your trust. I'll tell them I was wrong to share it." And he did, in front of everyone. No drama, no long sulk. We argued plenty after that, about films, politics, whose turn it was to pay, but we never lost each other. Forty years on, he still phones me on my birthday. At six in the morning, of course.

qa.q: What had Deepak told their friends that upset Bhavna?
qa.a: He had told them about Bhavna's failed exam.

qa.q: How did Deepak feel when Bhavna shouted at him, and what shows it?
qa.a: He seemed shaken and ashamed; he went pale.

qa.q: What choice did Deepak make the next day, and why did it work?
qa.a: He admitted he broke her trust and offered to tell the friends he was wrong, then did it, which repaired things without a long sulk.

qa.q: How might the other friends in the group have seen Deepak after he corrected himself in front of everyone?
qa.a: They likely saw him as someone who owns his mistakes, which would make him easier to trust with their own secrets.

grounding: An aunt recalls a college friend who kept his word, admitted breaking her trust and repaired it, so their many later arguments never ended the friendship.

passage: Forty minutes before the midnight deadline, the group's slides vanished: someone had saved over the shared file. Manjula watched the other three start blaming each other in the hostel common room, voices climbing. Imran, who had promised to do the final check, went pale, then said, "That was me. I saved the old copy over it. I'm sorry." Nobody spoke. He didn't argue or sulk; he opened his laptop. "I have most of it in my drafts. Give me the charts, I'll rebuild." Manjula noticed how the room cooled. They submitted at 11:58. Walking back, she remembered he had returned her notes on time all term. She wasn't sure she'd have owned up that fast.

qa.q: What time did the group submit?
qa.a: They submitted at 11:58.

qa.q: What was Manjula feeling as she walked back?
qa.a: She felt impressed and a little humbled, unsure she would have owned up as fast as Imran did.

qa.q: What could Manjula learn from how Imran handled the mistake?
qa.a: That admitting a mistake quickly and moving straight to fixing it calms a group better than blame.

qa.q: How might Imran have felt when he admitted the mistake?
qa.a: He was likely embarrassed and shaken, since he went pale, but he trusted the group enough to own it and start repairing.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone who admits a mistake and repairs it instead of turning it into a crisis.

passage: Rafiq had half expected Jomon to cancel. They'd had a stupid fight on Thursday about splitting a cab fare, and Jomon had gone quiet on the chat. But at seven on Sunday, as the tempo pulled up outside the Koramangala building, there was Jomon with a roll of tape and two samosas. "Said I'd help. So." They carried boxes up four floors. Halfway, Jomon set down a carton. "I was hurt about the cab thing. I also spoke badly. Can we sort it later, over tea?" Rafiq nodded, surprised. Most of his friends either sulked for weeks or pretended nothing had happened. Jomon did neither. By evening the flat was full of boxes, and the fight felt small.

qa.q: What did Jomon bring on Sunday?
qa.a: A roll of tape and two samosas.

qa.q: How did Rafiq feel when Jomon turned up and spoke about the fight?
qa.a: Rafiq felt surprised and relieved, because most friends sulked or pretended nothing happened, and Jomon did neither.

qa.q: What small step helped the two friends after the fight?
qa.a: Jomon kept the promise to help and named the hurt, then suggested sorting it later over tea instead of letting it grow.

qa.q: What is it like for Jomon to raise the fight halfway up the stairs?
qa.a: Jomon still feels hurt, yet chooses to say so and own the harsh words, which takes some courage.

grounding: Illustrates a friend noticing someone who keeps a promise and admits hurt without turning a disagreement into a crisis.

passage:
"You're late," Preeti said as Sachin dropped into the canteen chair.
"Twelve minutes. I said four; I'm sorry. The bus broke down near the bridge."
"You could have just said traffic."
"It was the bus. Also, about yesterday. I was short with you when you asked about the notes. That wasn't about you."
Preeti stirred her tea. "Kunal still hasn't spoken to me since our fight in March."
"Kunal treats every argument like a war. I'm not saying I didn't feel stung. I did. I'd rather say it and move on."
"Does it ever just stay stung?"
"Sometimes. Then I say that too."
Preeti smiled despite herself. In two years she had never once had to guess where she stood with Sachin.

qa.q: Why was Sachin late?
qa.a: The bus broke down near the bridge.

qa.q: What does Preeti's smile at the end suggest she feels?
qa.a: She feels reassured and grateful, noticing that with Sachin she never has to guess where she stands.

qa.q: What would you advise Preeti to take from this friendship?
qa.a: That saying a hurt plainly and then moving on keeps a friendship steady, unlike treating every argument as a war.

qa.q: How does Sachin see disagreements?
qa.a: Sachin admits feeling stung sometimes but prefers to say it and move on, rather than letting it become a crisis.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone who keeps promises, apologises and repairs rather than letting hurt become a crisis.

passage:
I've known Naveen since the first week of college, and it took me two years to notice what makes him different.
When he says he'll bring the notes, he brings them. When he forgot my birthday last March, he didn't make excuses. He came to my room the next day and said, "I messed up. I'm sorry." Then he stayed and helped me assemble a shelf.
Once we fought about a group project. I said something sharp. He went quiet and I could see it stung. But the next evening he knocked and said, "Can we sort this out?" No drama, no silent treatment for a week.
Honestly, I felt a bit jealous at first. I turn every argument into a disaster. Watching Naveen, I've started trying it his way: say the hurt, then fix it.
Avni, still practising

qa.q: What did Naveen do the day after forgetting the birthday?
qa.a: He said, "I messed up. I'm sorry," and stayed to help assemble a shelf.

qa.q: How did Avni feel when first noticing Naveen's steadiness?
qa.a: Avni felt a bit jealous, because Avni tends to turn every argument into a disaster.

qa.q: What could Avni learn from how Naveen handles fights?
qa.a: To say the hurt and then fix it: admit mistakes, come back to talk, and avoid long silent treatments.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Naveen after Avni's sharp remark?
qa.a: It clearly stung him, yet he came back the next evening to sort it out, showing that being hurt and repairing can go together.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing someone who keeps promises, admits mistakes and repairs after hurt, and wanting to learn from it.
